strengths: The paper addresses a practical and relevant problem: the quadratic cost of token-based visual world models during MPC rollouts, building on the DINO-WM line of work.

The experimental evaluation is fairly comprehensive: six environments, planning-time measurements, dropout-ratio sweeps, and a valuable comparative study showing that sophisticated token selection/pruning/merging methods (LTRP, STAR, EViT-style attention pruning, ATC) do not beat simple random sampling for planning.

The analysis sections (nHSIC mutual information, attentive probing, grouped attention ablations, CEM noise-robustness experiments) provide reasonable empirical support for why sparse token subsets suffice for planning, and the randomized grouped attention training strategy is shown to reduce subset prediction error.

The proposed method is simple and plug-in compatible with transformer world models, and the speed/performance trade-off via the dropout fraction is a practically useful knob; appendix provides good implementation detail supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea is essentially random patch dropout at inference time plus grouped-attention masks during training. Patch dropout for ViTs and token reduction methods are well established (the paper itself cites PatchDropout [29] and many pruning/merging works), so the contribution reads as an adaptation of known techniques to the world-model planning setting rather than a new insight.

Results are simulation-only, contradicting the stated motivation of real-time robotics deployment. Planning times of 80–300 s/iteration are far from real-time, and no real-robot or latency-constrained experiments are provided; the 'paving the way for real-time decision-making' claim is overstated.

Reported gains are modest and inconsistent: speedups at usable dropout ratios are roughly 30–50% (far below what the quadratic-cost argument would suggest for a 14x14 token grid), and several dropout settings underperform the Full baseline (e.g., Pointmaze 10–20% drop), while others exceed it (e.g., Granular 30% drop at 85% vs. 75% Full) with no statistical significance analysis to distinguish these fluctuations from noise.

The Full-Patch baseline is weak in some environments (e.g., Block Pushing at 22% success), and no comparison against other efficient world-model/planning approaches (e.g., latent low-dimensional world models beyond CLS, or other inference-acceleration techniques) is provided; baselines are limited to two variants of DINO-WM.

Only two groups in the randomized grouping training strategy, evaluated primarily with one encoder (DINO ViT-S/16); sensitivity to encoder choice and grouping granularity is unexplored, and the method requires per-environment tuning of the dropout rate.

Some analytical claims are loosely supported: the Gaussian-noise assumption for prediction error rests on visual inspection of UMAP plots, and the 'comparable or improved performance' claim is stronger than the mixed evidence in Table 1.

strengths: The paper is technically coherent and easy to follow, with a clearly stated research question about retaining patch-based world models while reducing planning cost.

A reasonably broad empirical study: six environments, two baselines (Full-Patch, CLS-Token), analysis via nHSIC, attentive probing, and an extensive comparison of token selection/merging strategies (LTRP, STAR, Attention-Encoder/WM, ATC, LHS).
The finding that simple random dropout matches or beats sophisticated token selection methods is a mildly interesting negative result, supported by appendix analysis (e.g., ATC overheads in Table 5).
Reasonably detailed implementation and appendix material supporting reproducibility of the setup.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea is inference-time random patch dropout, which is a direct adaptation of PatchDropout [29] and generic ViT token pruning literature to DINO-WM-style planning. The 'randomized grouped attention' training trick is essentially MAE-style masked training; the conceptual contribution is thin and positioning relative to [29] does not articulate what is fundamentally new.

The central claim of 'dramatically improving inference efficiency' is overstated. Table 2 shows ~30–50% planning-time reductions at the moderate dropout ratios where performance holds, and absolute planning times remain 40–300 s/iteration — far from real-time, contradicting the abstract's motivation about real-time/robotics deployment.

Performance results are noisy and inconsistent: at low dropout ratios (10–20%), random dropout sometimes outperforms Full by large margins (e.g., 28.0% vs 22.0% on Block Pushing, 73.3% vs 63.3% on Rope), which suggests high evaluation variance rather than a real effect. No error bars, confidence intervals, or seeds are reported in Tables 1–3, and only 20–60 evaluation episodes per environment; the key conclusions (comparable or improved performance under dropout) are not statistically supported.

Baselines are weak: only two baselines drawn from DINO-WM [7]. There is no comparison to alternative efficiency approaches (e.g., smaller encoders, reduced-resolution patches, KV-cache/latency optimizations, action chunking), so it is unclear whether token dropout is the right tool for the claimed problem.

Evaluation is simulation-only (acknowledged in limitations), on a fairly similar family of goal-conditioned pushing/navigation tasks; the practical significance for the robotics setting motivating the paper is not established.

Several claims are under-supported or hedged with circular reasoning: 'planning robustness' is argued by asserting CEM noise robustness plus a synthetic Gaussian-noise experiment justified only by visual inspection of UMAP plots; grouped attention benefits are shown only on one environment (Fig. 4) in the main text, with mixed success-rate improvements across dropout ratios.

The dropout rate p is a hand-tuned, environment-specific hyperparameter (best ratio varies from ~10% to ~50% across tasks), limiting the practicality of the method and weakening the 'adaptive to computational resource' claim in the abstract — there is no adaptive mechanism selecting p.

Writing issues: misleading framing ('decades or hundreds of tokens'), inconsistent notation/claims (e.g., exponential cost scaling with token count is incorrect — attention scales quadratically), a stray comma in the Figure 2 caption, and 'Demonstations' typo, suggesting insufficient polish.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical problem: the quadratic computational cost of patch-token world models (e.g., DINO-WM) during MPC planning, which limits real-time deployment.

The proposed method is simple, clean, and easy to implement: random token dropout at inference time, combined with randomized grouped attention during training to make the world model robust to arbitrary token subsets.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this type of method: six environments spanning navigation, pushing, and deformable-object manipulation; success-rate and wall-clock planning-time trade-offs across a full range of dropout ratios; and the finding that moderate dropout (10-50%) matches or exceeds the Full-Patch baseline while cutting planning time by ~30-50%.

The empirical analysis (nHSIC mutual information, attentive probing, grouped-attention ablation, CEM robustness-to-noise experiments) provides credible mechanistic support for why sparse rollout remains effective.

The comparative study of 8 token selection/merging strategies (LHS, LTRP, attention-based pruning, STAR, ATC, etc.) showing that sophisticated methods do not beat uniform random sampling is a useful, well-executed negative result.
Limitations are honestly discussed (simulation only, encoder-specificity, per-environment tuning of dropout rate).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. Random patch dropout is well established for ViTs (e.g., PatchDropout [29], MAE-style masking), and the world model is essentially DINO-WM [7]. The core contribution is applying token dropout during the imagination phase plus a simple two-group attention-mask training trick; the conceptual jump over prior token-efficiency work is small.

The headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The abstract/conclusion describe 'dramatically improving inference efficiency' and 'paving the way for deployment in real-time decision-making scenarios,' yet planning times remain 38-297 s per iteration even with 90% dropout, and the maximum speedup vs. Full-Patch is only ~50-78%. This is nowhere near real-time control, and the CLS baseline is still substantially faster.

Performance gains over the Full-Patch baseline are inconsistent and modest. In several environments (Pointmaze at low drop ratios, PushT at most ratios, Block Pushing overall) dropout performs equal to or worse than Full; in Block Pushing, even Full only achieves 22%, and small evaluation sets (20-30 episodes for Granular/Rope) make differences of a few percentage points hard to interpret. No statistical significance testing is reported.

The speedup is bounded by the choice of architecture: no comparison against more natural efficiency baselines such as a lower-resolution encoder, larger patch size, fewer layers, or a smaller ViT backbone, which could achieve similar token-count reductions without any special training scheme.
All experiments are in simulation with offline, mostly procedurally-generated or scripted datasets; no real-robot results despite the robotics/real-time motivation being the central selling point.

Baseline coverage beyond the token-selection axis is thin: only Full-Patch and CLS-Token are compared, both from the same DINO-WM paradigm; no comparison with latent-vector world models (Dreamer-family) or other efficient planning methods.

The dropout fraction p must be tuned per environment and per computational budget, which weakens the practical 'adaptively adjust based on resources' claim; no principled or automatic selection mechanism is provided.

Writing has noticeable typos/grammatical issues (e.g., 'decision masking', 'Visual Demonstations', Figure 2 caption comma), and some claims (e.g., computational cost 'scales exponentially with the number of visual tokens') are technically imprecise.

strengths: Practical and useful contribution: token dropout during latent imagination with a randomized grouped-attention training scheme gives roughly 40-50% planning-time reduction at 50% drop with near-baseline success rates, which is directly relevant for real-time robotic planning.

Unusually broad empirical validation: eight simulated environments plus real-robot tasks (SO-101) and integration with a modern VLA (SmolVLA) on LIBERO-10 and Meta-World, spanning three planning schemes (MPC-CEM, open-loop CEM, policy-guided planning).

Comprehensive and fair comparison of token-selection strategies (Random, Fixed, LHS, LTRP, attention-based, STAR, ATC) under a shared world model and hyperparameters, with careful implementation details for each adapted baseline.

Thoughtful analysis section: the 'blind spot' explanation for why static importance metrics fail in dynamic planning is supported by a targeted control experiment (21.7% vs 58.3% success) and quantitative blind-spot occurrence rates (Table 12); information-theoretic analyses (nHSIC, attentive probing) and cluster retention entropy further support the redundancy claim.

Extensive ablations in the appendix: grouped attention vs full attention prediction error, noise robustness of CEM, latency profiling confirming self-attention as the dominant cost, gradient-based planner (MPC-GD), longer horizons, adaptive dropout variants, and multiple vision encoders (DINO, MoCo-v3, MAE, DINOv3).
Honest limitations section and a strong reproducibility statement with detailed appendices.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core ingredients (patch dropout during training and inference, attention masking) closely resemble PatchDropout and other ViT token-reduction techniques; the contribution is primarily adapting them to world-model rollout/planning rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Baseline anomalies are not fully explained: 10-30% dropout often outperforms the full-token baseline (avg 74.1 vs 69.8), suggesting the method benefits from noise regularization, but this effect is not analyzed; no error bars or variance estimates are reported in Tables 1 and 4, making small differences hard to assess.

Statistically weak headline claims in the real-world and VLA experiments: the PickPlace/Drawer improvements are based on only 10 trials per task, and the LIBERO-10 gain (29% to 33%, 100 trials) is modest; describing a 60%-to-80% change on 10 trials as 'significant' overstates the evidence.

The speed-accuracy trade-off is environment-dependent: performance degrades sharply beyond ~60% drop in some tasks (PushT, Block Pushing) while Wall is almost insensitive, so the chosen operating point requires per-task tuning; the fixed dropout ratio limitation is acknowledged but only preliminarily addressed.

Absolute wall-clock numbers are very large (e.g., 82s per planning iteration in PushT even at 50% drop), which weakens the 'real-time' deployment narrative in simulation, though the real-robot experiments partially mitigate this via asynchronous inference.

The blind-spot analysis, while insightful, is largely empirical and specific to importance-based masking; no formal characterization or theory of when random sparsification suffices for planning is provided.

strengths: The paper is well-organized and clearly written, with a simple, easy-to-understand core idea (random token dropout during world-model rollout) that is attractive for resource-constrained robotics.

The empirical coverage is broad: eight simulated environments plus two real-world SO-101 tasks, three planning schemes (MPC-CEM, open-loop CEM, VLA-guided planning), and multiple pre-trained encoders (DINO, MoCo-v3, MAE, DINOv3).

The comparative study of token-selection strategies (Section 4.4, Table 4) and the 'blind spot' analysis (Section 5.4, Appendix B.9) are the most interesting parts of the paper — the quantitative blind-spot occurrence rates (Table 12) and the counter-intuitive finding that importance-based selection fails in dynamic planning provide a genuinely useful insight for future work on token reduction in control.

Thorough appendices: hyperparameter ablations (CEM steps, planning horizon, frame skip), latency profiling (Table 11), adaptive dropout exploration (B.6), and LPIPS checks confirming the training strategy does not degrade prediction quality.
Randomized grouped attention during training is a reasonable design choice, and the ablation (Fig. 4, Fig. 11) supports its necessity for sparse-input robustness.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. Random patch dropout during training is well established (PatchDropout, Liu et al., 2023b, which the authors themselves cite), and the contribution here is largely a re-application of that idea at inference time in a DINO-WM-style pipeline. The 'randomized grouped attention' training strategy is essentially a variant of training-time token dropout, and the paper's own conclusion that 'simple random sampling is the best strategy' somewhat undercuts the novelty of the method itself.

The main results raise variance and reliability concerns. In Table 1, several sparse settings (e.g., 10% drop avg. 74.1, 30% drop 71.0) *outperform* the Full baseline (69.8), which is hard to explain without substantial variance; yet no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported for the main tables. Eval counts are small (20–60 episodes; 10 trials per real-world task), making fine-grained claims (e.g., 'Drop 50% 47.73 vs Full 48.80' in Table 3) statistically fragile.

The evaluation of the headline efficiency claim is not fully convincing. Planning takes 73–297 seconds per iteration even with sparse imagination (Table 2) — far from real-time; the savings are mostly relevant only for the expensive Full-Patch planner, which is itself a somewhat artificial strawman. Speedups at 90% drop approach the CLS baseline's cost while performing worse than Full in several environments.

Inconsistencies across tables are not explained. E.g., Random sampling achieves 50.4 on PushT in Table 4 while the 50% drop row in Table 1 shows 70.0; the averaging/protocol differences are only partially clarified, making cross-table comparison confusing.

The mismatch between training (two spatial groups) and inference (arbitrary subsets) is only loosely justified; the paper does not explain why training with actual random dropout masks of varying rates was not done or how it would compare.

The 'general technique applicable to VLAs' framing is overclaimed: the VLA-guided results rely on SmolVLA with modified action-chunk execution (executing all 50 actions despite acknowledged lower absolute performance), and the LIBERO-10 improvement (29% to 33%) is modest with only 100 trials. The Meta-World gain over VLA-only (41.87 to 47.73) also carries wide uncertainty.

The blind-spot finding, while interesting, mostly serves as a negative result about importance-based token selection; it motivates but does not itself constitute a strong methodological contribution, and the proposed remedy is simply 'use random dropout,' which any practitioner would likely try first.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: quadratic cost of token-based world model rollouts during MPC/CEM planning is a real bottleneck for robotics deployment, and the paper directly targets inference-time efficiency rather than training cost.

The method is simple, general, and essentially plug-and-play (token dropout at inference + randomized grouped attention at training), and the paper convincingly demonstrates applicability across planning paradigms (MPC-CEM, open-loop CEM, policy/VLA-guided planning, and a gradient-based MPC-GD planner in Appendix B.5).

Unusually broad empirical coverage: eight simulated environments (Pointmaze, Wall, PushT, Granular, Rope, Block Pushing, LIBERO-10, Meta-World) plus real-world SO-101 experiments, with latency measurements at each drop ratio (Table 2) and a fine-grained latency breakdown (Table 11).

The comparative study of token selection families (random, LHS, learned pruning LTRP, attention-based STAR/Attention-Encoder/Attention-WM, clustering ATC) is a valuable contribution, and the 'blind spot' analysis (Section 5.4, Table 12, Fig. 9/20) provides a plausible, quantitatively supported explanation for why static importance metrics fail in dynamic planning.

Supporting analyses strengthen the claims: nHSIC and attentive probing (Figs. 7-8) show state information is distributed across tokens; ablations confirm grouped attention reduces prediction error under sparsity (Fig. 4, Fig. 11); LPIPS analysis (Table 10) shows training with grouped attention does not degrade full-patch prediction quality; adaptive-dropout feasibility study (Table 9) is a nice extra.
Good reproducibility posture: detailed appendix with dataset configurations, hyperparameters, planning details, and reproduction pointers for baseline token-reduction methods.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: random patch dropout during inference is well established in vision (PatchDropout, MAE-style masked training, DynamicViT, etc.), and the core contribution is largely an application of these ideas to the planning/rollout stage of a DINO-WM-style world model plus a grouped-attention training trick. The paper itself concedes random sampling is the best strategy, which makes the 'method' essentially a strong baseline rather than a new technique.

Headline gains on the most complex tasks are modest and potentially within noise: LIBERO-10 improves only from 29% to 33% (VLA-only to 50% drop; Fig. 5 shows 27-33% band), and Meta-World gains over Full are marginal (Table 3). No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for Table 1 or Table 3, despite evident non-monotonicity (e.g., 10% drop beating Full in several environments, and Block Pushing showing erratic behavior), making some improvements hard to attribute to the method.

Absolute planning latency is concerning for the claimed 'real-time' positioning: planning times of 173s per iteration (PushT) and ~90s even at 50% drop are far from real-time; fixed costs (encoder + env step + others, ~25s per Table 11) dominate at high drop ratios, so the speedup curve flattens and the practicality argument for real-time robotic deployment is weakened. The real-world 'gain' over Full-Patch partly reflects that the Full-Patch planner is simply too slow to finish episodes.

Real-world evaluation is small and somewhat hand-tuned: only 10 trials per task, fixed cup/drawer poses for data collection, manually selected goal images and proprioceptive goal states, and Drawer testing uses block positions included in training. Statistical support for the 60%→80% / 70% success claims is thin.

The speedup in Table 2 is substantially smaller than the theoretical quadratic gain (e.g., only ~30-43% wall-clock reduction at 50% drop on some environments), and comparisons to the CLS-token baseline, while favorable, mainly show that extreme compression fails — leaving open the question of cheaper intermediate alternatives (e.g., 2x2 patch merging, lower-resolution encoders) that are not evaluated.

Writing/clarity issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('eight simulated environment', 'impractial', 'apporaches'), Table 4's averaging protocol for excluded cells is confusingly described, and the claim that results 'consistently show none of these methods significantly outperform random sampling' is stated without statistical testing.
